topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under general national real property doctrine, a fee simple absolute is best described as:
choice_a: An ownership interest that automatically ends if a stated condition occurs
choice_b: The most complete form of ownership, potentially lasting forever and freely transferable, with no conditions limiting its duration
choice_c: An estate that lasts only for the life of the current owner
choice_d: A possessory interest created by a lease rather than by a deed
explanation: A fee simple absolute is the highest and most complete form of ownership recognized at law -- it has an indefinite duration and no conditions or limitations restricting it.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A fee simple determinable is created by language such as 'so long as,' 'while,' or 'during,' and differs from a fee simple absolute because:
choice_a: The grantee must first record a new deed before title can revert
choice_b: The estate can never be inherited by the grantee's heirs
choice_c: Title automatically reverts to the grantor (or grantor's heirs) the instant the stated condition is violated, without any action needed by the grantor
choice_d: The grantor must first win a lawsuit before regaining title
explanation: A fee simple determinable automatically terminates and reverts to the grantor (holding a 'possibility of reverter') the moment the stated condition is broken -- no re-entry action by the grantor is required.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A fee simple subject to condition subsequent differs from a fee simple determinable primarily in that:
choice_a: It is not a form of fee simple estate at all
choice_b: It cannot be created by a deed, only by a will
choice_c: The grantee has no interest until the grantor dies
choice_d: Title does not automatically revert when the condition is broken -- the grantor must affirmatively exercise a 'right of reentry' to retake the property
explanation: Unlike a fee simple determinable's automatic reversion, a fee simple subject to condition subsequent gives the grantor a 'right of reentry' (power of termination) that must be affirmatively exercised to retake title after the condition is broken.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A life estate is an ownership interest that:
choice_a: Lasts for the duration of a specified person's life, after which it terminates and the property passes to a remainderman or reverts to the grantor
choice_b: Lasts forever and passes to the life tenant's heirs at death
choice_c: Automatically converts to a leasehold after five years
choice_d: Cannot be created unless the life tenant pays the grantor rent
explanation: A life estate is a freehold estate whose duration is measured by a specified person's lifetime; when that measuring life ends, the estate terminates and title passes to a remainderman or reverts to the grantor.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A life estate 'pur autre vie' is measured by:
choice_a: The life of the life tenant only
choice_b: The life of someone other than the life tenant
choice_c: A fixed term of 99 years
choice_d: The life of the grantor's youngest heir
explanation: A life estate 'pur autre vie' (French for 'for the life of another') is measured not by the life tenant's own life, but by the life of a different, named person.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: When a life estate is created and the property is designated to pass to a named third party once the life estate ends, that third party holds a:
choice_a: Reversion -- because it returns to the original grantor
choice_b: Leasehold estate
choice_c: Remainder interest -- a future interest that vests in someone other than the grantor when the life estate terminates
choice_d: Present possessory fee simple
explanation: A remainder is a future interest held by a third party (not the grantor) that becomes possessory automatically when a preceding estate, such as a life estate, ends.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: If a life estate is created without naming a third-party beneficiary to take the property afterward, the interest that automatically returns to the grantor (or the grantor's heirs) when the life estate ends is called a:
choice_a: Remainder
choice_b: Escheat
choice_c: Easement in gross
choice_d: Reversion
explanation: A reversion is the future interest retained by a grantor (or the grantor's heirs) when a lesser estate, such as a life estate, is conveyed and no third-party remainderman is named.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Compared to a fee simple estate, a life estate is generally considered less marketable primarily because:
choice_a: Its duration is uncertain and tied to a measuring life, and it terminates automatically at that person's death, limiting what a buyer or lender receives
choice_b: Life estates cannot legally be sold at all
choice_c: Life estates always require government approval to transfer
choice_d: Life estates are only recognized in a handful of states
explanation: Because a life estate's duration depends on an uncertain measuring life and terminates automatically at death, buyers and lenders receive an inherently limited and less marketable interest compared to a fee simple.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: The key distinction between a freehold estate and a leasehold estate is that a freehold estate:
choice_a: Can never be transferred to another party
choice_b: Involves ownership of the property for an indeterminate or lifetime duration, while a leasehold is merely a right to possess for a defined term
choice_c: Only exists in commercial (not residential) real estate
choice_d: Requires the owner to also hold a professional real estate license
explanation: A freehold estate (fee simple or life estate) is an ownership interest of indeterminate duration, whereas a leasehold is a non-ownership possessory interest limited to a defined lease term.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: The 'bundle of rights' concept in real property law refers to:
choice_a: A single indivisible right that cannot be separated or transferred individually
choice_b: The physical materials (soil, minerals, structures) that make up the land
choice_c: The set of legal rights associated with property ownership, including the rights to possess, use, transfer, encumber, and exclude others from the property
choice_d: A government-issued bundle of permits required before construction
explanation: The 'bundle of rights' describes ownership as a collection of separate legal rights -- including possession, use, transfer, encumbrance, and exclusion -- that can be held together or separately conveyed.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (property ownership)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Whether an item that was once personal property (chattel) has become a fixture -- and therefore transfers with the real property -- generally depends on factors such as:
choice_a: Only the item's original purchase price
choice_b: Only whether the item is made of metal or wood
choice_c: Only which spouse purchased the item
choice_d: The method of attachment, adaptation to the property's use, and the parties' intent
explanation: Courts generally weigh the method and permanence of attachment, the item's adaptation to the property's use, and the parties' intent to determine whether a chattel has become a fixture.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (property ownership)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A 'trade fixture' installed by a commercial tenant for business purposes:
choice_a: Remains the tenant's personal property and may generally be removed before the lease term ends, unlike an ordinary fixture
choice_b: Automatically becomes the landlord's property the moment it is installed
choice_c: Can never be removed under any circumstances
choice_d: Converts the tenant's leasehold into a fee simple estate
explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a business tenant remain that tenant's personal property and are generally removable before the lease expires, an exception to the ordinary rule that attached fixtures pass with the real property.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (property ownership)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under common-law doctrine, creating a valid joint tenancy traditionally requires the 'four unities' of:
choice_a: Age, income, marital status, and citizenship
choice_b: Time, title, interest, and possession -- all joint tenants must acquire their interests at the same time, by the same instrument, with equal interests, and equal rights to possession
choice_c: Race, gender, religion, and national origin
choice_d: Location, zoning, survey, and appraisal
explanation: The traditional common-law 'four unities' required to create a joint tenancy are time, title, interest, and possession -- each joint tenant must acquire an equal interest at the same time, via the same instrument, with equal rights to possess the whole.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (concurrent ownership)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: If one of three joint tenants conveys (sells) their interest to a new, unrelated buyer, the general effect on that particular interest is that:
choice_a: The entire joint tenancy is automatically dissolved and the property is sold at auction
choice_b: The sale is void because joint tenancy interests cannot be conveyed
choice_c: The conveyance severs the joint tenancy as to that share -- the new buyer typically becomes a tenant in common with the remaining original joint tenants, who continue to hold a joint tenancy among themselves
choice_d: The buyer automatically inherits full ownership if any original tenant later dies
explanation: Conveying a joint tenant's interest to an outside party severs the joint tenancy as to that interest; the new owner generally holds as a tenant in common, while any remaining original joint tenants continue their joint tenancy among themselves.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (concurrent ownership)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: In several other states, spouses may hold title together as 'tenants by the entirety,' a form of ownership with survivorship rights available only to married couples. Since Wisconsin adopted its Marital Property Act (Wis. Stat. ch. 766, effective 1986), property held by spouses is generally classified instead as:
choice_a: A leasehold estate held jointly by both spouses
choice_b: Property that automatically escheats to the state
choice_c: A trade fixture
choice_d: Marital property, governed by ch. 766, rather than under the traditional common-law tenancy-by-the-entirety form
explanation: Wisconsin's Marital Property Act, effective January 1, 1986, replaced the common-law tenancy-by-the-entirety framework recognized in some other states -- spousal ownership in Wisconsin is instead classified and governed as marital property under ch. 766.
source_note: Wis. Stat. ch. 766 (Marital Property Act); hedge: general comparison to national tenancy-by-the-entirety doctrine

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: 'Community property' is the marital-property ownership regime used by a number of other U.S. states (e.g., California, Texas). Wisconsin's analogous but independently codified regime for classifying spousal property is found at:
choice_a: Wis. Stat. Chapter 766, the Marital Property Act
choice_b: Wis. Stat. Chapter 706, governing conveyances
choice_c: Wis. Stat. Chapter 452, governing real estate licensees
choice_d: Wis. Admin. Code REEB 1-99
explanation: Wisconsin's Marital Property Act, Wis. Stat. ch. 766, is the state's own codified regime for classifying spousal property -- often compared to, but legally distinct from, the community property systems used in other states.
source_note: Wis. Stat. ch. 766 (Marital Property Act); hedge: general comparison to national community-property doctrine

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A 'metes and bounds' legal description identifies a parcel of land by:
choice_a: Referencing only a recorded subdivision plat's lot and block number
choice_b: Starting at a defined point of beginning and describing the boundary as a series of courses (directions) and distances back to that point of beginning
choice_c: Referencing only the property's street address
choice_d: Referencing only the township and range numbers, with no distances
explanation: A metes and bounds description traces a parcel's boundary as a series of courses and distances from a defined point of beginning, ultimately returning to that same point.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (legal descriptions)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under the U.S. government (rectangular) survey system, a standard township is a square parcel measuring approximately:
choice_a: 1 mile by 1 mile, divided into 4 quarter-sections
choice_b: 10 miles by 10 miles, divided into 100 sections
choice_c: 6 miles by 6 miles, divided into 36 sections of one square mile (640 acres) each
choice_d: A township has no fixed size and varies by county
explanation: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, a township is a 6-mile-by-6-mile square divided into 36 sections, each one square mile, or 640 acres.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (legal descriptions)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: The 'lot and block' method of legal description identifies a specific parcel by referencing:
choice_a: A metes-and-bounds course-and-distance survey only
choice_b: The parcel's GPS coordinates exclusively
choice_c: The township, range, and section numbers only
choice_d: The lot and block numbers shown on a recorded subdivision plat map filed with the county
explanation: The lot and block system identifies a parcel by its lot and block numbers as they appear on a recorded subdivision plat map filed with the county, which itself is tied to a metes-and-bounds or government survey description.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (legal descriptions)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Which of the following is generally required for a deed to be legally valid and effective at common law?
choice_a: A competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, a legal description of the property, and the grantor's signature, plus delivery and acceptance
choice_b: Notarization by two separate notaries in different counties
choice_c: Payment of the full purchase price in cash at the moment of signing
choice_d: Approval by the local real estate board
explanation: A valid deed generally requires a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, a legal description of the property, the grantor's signature, and delivery to and acceptance by the grantee.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (deed requirements)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A deed is not legally effective to transfer title merely by being signed by the grantor -- it must also be:
choice_a: Published in a local newspaper
choice_b: Delivered by the grantor with the intent to convey, and accepted by the grantee
choice_c: Co-signed by the grantee's lender
choice_d: Filed with the IRS
explanation: Title does not pass on signature alone -- a deed must also be delivered by the grantor with intent to convey, and accepted by the grantee, before the transfer of title is complete.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (deed requirements)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: The clause in a deed traditionally beginning 'to have and to hold,' which defines the type and extent of the estate being conveyed to the grantee, is known as the:
choice_a: Granting clause
choice_b: Defeasance clause
choice_c: Habendum clause
choice_d: Acceleration clause
explanation: The habendum clause, beginning 'to have and to hold,' defines and limits the estate and interest the grantee is receiving under the deed.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (deed requirements)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: To acquire title to land through adverse possession, a claimant must generally show possession that is:
choice_a: Secret and hidden from the record owner for at least one year
choice_b: Permitted in writing by the record owner
choice_c: Limited to weekend or seasonal use only
choice_d: Open and notorious, hostile (without the owner's permission), actual, exclusive, and continuous for the statutory period
explanation: Adverse possession generally requires possession that is open and notorious, hostile to the true owner's title, actual, exclusive, and continuous throughout the applicable statutory period.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (adverse possession)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: If a claimant satisfies all elements of adverse possession for the full statutory period, the legal result is that:
choice_a: The claimant can acquire title to the property, generally without having to pay the original record owner any compensation
choice_b: The claimant must still purchase the property at fair market value
choice_c: The claimant gains only a temporary leasehold, never fee title
choice_d: The original owner automatically regains title regardless of the claimant's possession
explanation: When all elements of adverse possession are met for the statutory period, the claimant can acquire legal title to the property without compensating the original record owner.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (adverse possession)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: 'Eminent domain' refers to the government's power to:
choice_a: Seize property without any compensation whenever it chooses
choice_b: Take private property for a public use, provided the owner receives just compensation
choice_c: Revoke a real estate license for misconduct
choice_d: Foreclose on a defaulted mortgage
explanation: Eminent domain is the government's constitutional power to take private property for a public use, so long as the owner is paid just compensation.
source_note: REEB 25.033(9)(c) -- involuntary alienation (eminent domain)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: When a property owner dies without a valid will (intestate) and leaves no heirs who can be located or identified, title to the property generally passes to the state through a process called:
choice_a: Accretion
choice_b: Dedication
choice_c: Escheat
choice_d: Novation
explanation: Escheat is the process by which property reverts to the state when an owner dies intestate with no ascertainable heirs to inherit it.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (escheat)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: 'Accretion' is the process by which a riparian or littoral landowner's property boundary:
choice_a: Suddenly decreases due to a violent flood tearing away a large parcel of land
choice_b: Shifts due to a government re-survey
choice_c: Is fixed permanently regardless of any water movement
choice_d: Gradually increases as soil is naturally and imperceptibly deposited by the action of adjacent water
explanation: Accretion is the gradual, imperceptible buildup of soil along a waterfront property caused by natural water action, which increases the landowner's boundary.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (methods of acquiring/losing title)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: 'Avulsion' differs from accretion in that avulsion refers to:
choice_a: A sudden, perceptible loss (or gain) of land caused by a dramatic event such as a flood or a river suddenly changing course
choice_b: The slow, gradual buildup of soil along a riverbank over many years
choice_c: A landowner voluntarily dedicating land to the public
choice_d: A tenant's removal of trade fixtures at the end of a lease
explanation: Avulsion is a sudden and perceptible change in a boundary caused by a dramatic natural event, in contrast to accretion's slow and imperceptible gradual buildup.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (methods of acquiring/losing title)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: 'Dedication' of land occurs when:
choice_a: A court orders land seized for nonpayment of taxes
choice_b: A private landowner voluntarily transfers land (such as for a street or park) to public ownership or use
choice_c: A lender forecloses on a defaulted mortgage
choice_d: Two adjoining owners informally agree to share a driveway
explanation: Dedication is the voluntary transfer of privately owned land to public ownership or use, such as a developer dedicating streets within a subdivision to the municipality.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (methods of acquiring/losing title)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: The primary purpose of a public land-records recording system is to provide:
choice_a: A guarantee that the recorded document is free of forgery
choice_b: Proof that the property is free of physical defects
choice_c: Constructive notice to the world of recorded interests in real property, establishing priority among competing claims
choice_d: A mechanism for collecting property taxes
explanation: Recording a document gives constructive notice to the world of the recorded interest and helps establish priority among competing claims to the same property.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (recording system)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Recording statutes are generally classified as 'race,' 'notice,' or 'race-notice' statutes. Under a race-notice statute -- the type Wisconsin follows under Wis. Stat. 706.08 -- a subsequent purchaser is protected against a prior unrecorded conveyance only if that subsequent purchaser:
choice_a: Simply recorded first, regardless of notice or good faith
choice_b: Simply had no notice of the prior conveyance, regardless of who recorded first
choice_c: Paid the highest price among competing purchasers
choice_d: Took in good faith without notice of the prior conveyance AND recorded first
explanation: Under a race-notice recording statute such as Wisconsin's Wis. Stat. 706.08, a subsequent purchaser is protected only if they both took in good faith without notice of the prior conveyance AND won the 'race' to record first.
source_note: Wis. Stat. 706.08; hedge: general recording-statute doctrine (race/notice/race-notice classifications)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: The complete, chronological history of recorded documents affecting title to a specific parcel is called its:
choice_a: Chain of title
choice_b: Habendum clause
choice_c: Bundle of rights
choice_d: Escheat record
explanation: The chain of title is the chronological sequence of recorded documents (deeds, mortgages, liens, etc.) that reflects the successive transfers and encumbrances affecting a specific parcel.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (recording system)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A 'cloud on title' refers to:
choice_a: A title that has been confirmed free of all defects by a court
choice_b: Any recorded document, claim, or defect that casts doubt on the validity or marketability of an owner's title
choice_c: A weather-related restriction on outdoor property improvements
choice_d: A deed that has not yet been signed
explanation: A cloud on title is any outstanding claim, encumbrance, or defect of record that casts doubt on the validity or marketability of an owner's title, often requiring a quitclaim deed or quiet title action to clear.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (recording system)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: 'Riparian rights' are water-use rights associated with land bordering:
choice_a: A non-flowing waterbody such as a lake or ocean (which instead involves 'littoral' rights)
choice_b: Underground aquifers only, regardless of surface water
choice_c: A flowing waterbody such as a river or stream
choice_d: Any body of water located more than one mile from the property
explanation: Riparian rights pertain to land bordering a flowing waterbody such as a river or stream, while 'littoral' rights are the analogous term used for land bordering non-flowing waterbodies such as lakes or oceans.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (water rights)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Ownership of a condominium unit typically combines:
choice_a: A leasehold interest in the unit with no ownership interest in any common areas
choice_b: Shares in a corporation that owns the entire building, plus a proprietary lease
choice_c: A life estate in the unit that terminates when the owner dies
choice_d: Fee simple (or similar) ownership of the individual unit's interior airspace with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the building's common elements
explanation: Condominium ownership generally combines fee simple (or similar) ownership of the individual unit's airspace with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest, shared with other unit owners, in the building's common elements.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (forms of ownership)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Cooperative ('co-op') ownership differs from condominium ownership primarily in that in a cooperative, the resident:
choice_a: Owns shares in a corporation that holds title to the entire building, and occupies a unit under a proprietary lease from that corporation
choice_b: Directly owns fee simple title to their individual unit
choice_c: Holds only an easement in gross over the unit
choice_d: Automatically becomes a joint tenant with every other resident
explanation: In a cooperative, the resident does not directly own real property; instead, they own shares in a corporation that holds title to the whole building, and they occupy their unit under a proprietary lease from that corporation.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (forms of ownership)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A 'homestead' exemption or designation generally provides an owner-occupant with legal protections such as:
choice_a: Automatic exemption from all property taxes
choice_b: Limiting the ability of certain creditors to force the sale of the owner's primary residence to satisfy debts, up to a statutory exemption amount
choice_c: A guarantee of a minimum resale price
choice_d: Elimination of the need to record the deed
explanation: A homestead exemption or designation generally protects an owner-occupant's primary residence, up to a statutory dollar amount, from being forcibly sold to satisfy certain creditors' claims.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (property protections)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: The term 'encumbrance' is broader than the term 'lien' because an encumbrance includes:
choice_a: Only unpaid mortgage debt
choice_b: Only unpaid property taxes
choice_c: Any claim, right, or interest that burdens title -- including monetary liens as well as non-monetary matters such as easements and deed restrictions
choice_d: Only claims filed by a spouse under marital property law
explanation: An 'encumbrance' is the broader term, covering any claim or right burdening title -- monetary liens as well as non-monetary matters like easements, encroachments, and deed restrictions -- while a 'lien' is specifically a monetary claim.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (title burdens)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A life tenant's legal duty not to permanently damage or diminish the value of the property to the detriment of the remainderman or reversioner is known as the doctrine against:
choice_a: Escheat
choice_b: Dedication
choice_c: Avulsion
choice_d: Waste
explanation: The doctrine against waste obligates a life tenant to reasonably maintain the property and refrain from actions that would permanently damage or diminish its value for the remainderman or reversioner who will take possession afterward.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (estates in land)

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A 'bargain and sale deed' differs from a general or special warranty deed in that it:
choice_a: Implies the grantor holds title to convey but includes no express covenants warranting against encumbrances or defects
choice_b: Conveys no interest at all, unless separately recorded
choice_c: Can only be used to transfer leasehold interests
choice_d: Requires the buyer to assume the seller's existing mortgage
explanation: A bargain and sale deed implies that the grantor holds title to the property but, unlike a warranty deed, includes no express covenants warranting against liens, encumbrances, or other title defects.
source_note: REEB 25.033(9)(b) -- types of deeds (bargain and sale deed)
